problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 1, including the stated time-dilation and Lorentz-FitzGerald-contraction results and the operational meaning of 'appear': derive relativity of simultaneity for a moving train in part (a) by front-to-rear light-pulse synchronization and in part (b) by slowly carrying one initially colocated clock to the rear, without using a Lorentz transformation.
problems.short_topic: Relativity of simultaneity from clock-synchronization experiments
problems.disposition_rationale: A detailed, self-contained Chapter 2 parent that derives the synchronization offset by two physically distinct procedures. The supplied kinematic facts, train setup, prohibition on assuming Lorentz transformations, and limiting slow-transport argument are all essential.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 2: impose the printed periodic identifications of a spatial three-torus of size L, compare an observer at rest with one moving inertially once around the x direction until their worldlines meet again, calculate both proper times, and reconcile the result with Lorentz invariance.
problems.short_topic: Twin effect with spatially periodic boundary conditions
problems.disposition_rationale: This compact but conceptually strong Chapter 2 parent separates local Lorentz invariance from global boundary conditions. The full three-torus identification and the no-acceleration reunion are necessary to resolve the apparent twin-paradox tension.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 3, parts (a)-(d): prove the existence of rest frames for timelike-separated events and simultaneity frames for spacelike-separated events; prove that the sum of orthogonal spacelike vectors is spacelike; and prove that a timelike vector cannot be orthogonal to a null vector.
problems.short_topic: Causal classes and orthogonality of Lorentz vectors
problems.disposition_rationale: The four short claims form one coherent exercise on Lorentzian causal geometry for Chapter 2. Keeping them together tests both frame construction and invariant arguments rather than isolated sign manipulations.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 4: given observers who see three events in the orders ABC and CBA, decide whether a third inertial observer can see ACB and support the conclusion with a spacetime diagram.
problems.short_topic: Observer-dependent ordering of three events
problems.disposition_rationale: A bounded causal-order problem for Chapter 2 whose requested diagram is part of the parent. No figure is supplied, so the source-compatible spacetime diagram must be constructed rather than omitted.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 5, using the printed nonsymmetric 4-by-4 tensor X^{mu nu}, vector V^mu, and symmetrization definitions: compute parts (a)-(g), namely X^mu_nu, X_mu^nu, X^{(mu nu)}, X^{[mu nu]}, the trace X^lambda_lambda, the norm V^mu V_mu, and the contraction V_mu X^{mu nu}, retaining the matrix-display guidance.
problems.short_topic: Numerical Lorentz-index manipulation
problems.disposition_rationale: This is an elementary numerical component drill with no physical or geometric development beyond raising, lowering, symmetrizing, tracing, and contracting a supplied matrix. Weinberg's Chapter 2 is better served by invariant parents, so the complete problem is inventoried but not reserved.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 6: in part (a) apply the tensor transformation of F_{mu nu} to derive electric- and magnetic-field transformations under a z boost; in part (b) transform the uniform field of a large positively charged sheet for an observer moving along x, check against electromagnetic source transformations, and describe a negative test charge's motion in both frames.
problems.short_topic: Electric and magnetic fields under Lorentz boosts
problems.disposition_rationale: A strong Chapter 2 parent linking the field-strength tensor to transformed sources and particle motion. Both the general boost calculation and the charged-sheet application, including the two-frame interpretation, must remain together.

documents.institution_or_author: Alan Guth, Massachusetts Institute of Technology

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 1, parts (a)-(c), for the printed two-sphere metric: rotate an equatorial great circle and derive its coordinate equations; derive the geodesic differential equations using either supplied form while deciding whether psi is proportional to arc length; and verify the rotated great circles using the two supplied derivative hints.
problems.short_topic: Great-circle geodesics on a two-sphere
problems.disposition_rationale: This complete Chapter 4 parent connects an extrinsic rotation construction with intrinsic geodesic equations and parameterization. The metric's printed overall form, both alternative geodesic formulas, and the derivative hint are integral source content.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 2: transform between Cartesian and polar coordinates in the Euclidean plane, find the geodesic r(lambda), theta(lambda) joining (1,0) to (2,pi/3), compute the Christoffel symbols, and verify the path against the printed affinely parameterized geodesic equation.
problems.short_topic: Flat-space geodesics in polar coordinates
problems.disposition_rationale: Although introductory, this is a self-contained Chapter 4 check that a nonzero coordinate connection in polar coordinates describes flat geometry. The fixed endpoints and explicit Christoffel verification keep it from being a mere formula-recall exercise.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 3, parts (a)-(d), for ds^2=(1+3x^2)^2(dx^2+dy^2): compute the straight-line distance between p=(-1,-2) and q=(1,2); derive the geodesic equation and disprove that trajectory even with proper parameterization; exhibit a shorter path made of three straight pieces using the supplied 'cheapest region' hint; and sketch the actual geodesic qualitatively.
problems.short_topic: Geodesic intuition in an inhomogeneous conformal metric
problems.disposition_rationale: A useful Chapter 4 parent that contrasts coordinate-straight paths, length minimization, and geodesic equations in a position-dependent metric. All four stages and the path-construction hint are needed for its pedagogical point.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 4, parts (a)-(d), for the upper-half-plane metric y^{-2}(dx^2+dy^2): calculate the infinite distance to y=0; compute every Christoffel component and the geodesic equations; prove vertical lines and boundary-centered semicircles are geodesics; and retain the concluding comparison with Euclid's parallel postulate.
problems.short_topic: Geodesics of the hyperbolic upper half-plane
problems.disposition_rationale: This is a complete geometric model of a maximally symmetric negative-curvature space for Chapter 13. The boundary-at-infinite-distance result, two families of geodesics, and non-Euclidean parallel interpretation form one indivisible parent.

documents.institution_or_author: Alan Guth, Massachusetts Institute of Technology

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 1, parts (a)-(h): derive induced metrics in polar and Cartesian descriptions of a general graph z=f; verify their coordinate equivalence; specialize to a paraboloid and a cone and compute both connections; construct the specified conical geodesic using the coordinate-simplification hint; and find the cone parameter for which it self-crosses orthogonally.
problems.short_topic: Metrics and geodesics of rotational embedding surfaces
problems.disposition_rationale: A substantial Chapter 6 parent connecting induced metrics, coordinate transformations, connections, and global conical geodesics. The paraboloid and cone specializations and the right-angle self-intersection endpoint are connected stages and cannot be split.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 2, parts (a)-(c), for g_00=-(1+az), g_0i=0, g_ij=delta_ij near the origin: find all nonzero Christoffel symbols; derive the leading acceleration of a slowly moving particle initially at the origin; and construct the printed quadratic coordinate transformation to a local inertial system, explaining its physical meaning.
problems.short_topic: Local inertial coordinates in a Newtonian field
problems.disposition_rationale: This is a strong Chapter 3 parent that explicitly demonstrates the equivalence principle at connection and coordinate levels. The weak-field condition, initial data, quadratic transformation ansatz, and physical interpretation are all required.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 3: transform the printed flat cylindrical metric to coordinates rotating with angular speed omega in part (a); then in part (b) compute the full connection and geodesic equations and identify their small-omega-r centripetal and Coriolis terms.
problems.short_topic: Rotating coordinates and inertial forces
problems.disposition_rationale: A clean Chapter 3 application showing how gravitational-looking forces arise from a noninertial coordinate system in flat spacetime. Both the exact rotating metric and the low-speed force interpretation must be preserved.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 4: using either of the two printed forms of the geodesic equation, prove that A=g_{mu nu}(dx^mu/dlambda)(dx^nu/dlambda) is constant and deduce that a geodesic cannot change between null, timelike, and spacelike causal type.
problems.short_topic: Affine parameterization and conserved tangent norm
problems.disposition_rationale: This concise but substantive Chapter 4 parent closes a logical gap in the variational derivation of affinely parameterized geodesics. Both alternative equations and the causal-type consequence are explicit parts of the source.

documents.institution_or_author: Alan Guth, Massachusetts Institute of Technology

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 1: starting from the supplied count of components of a fully symmetric rank-R tensor in D dimensions, derive the number of independent components of a fully antisymmetric rank-R tensor.
problems.short_topic: Counting antisymmetric tensor components
problems.disposition_rationale: The parent is a single combinatorial formula exercise without geometric or gravitational application. It is accurately inventoried but is too slight to displace stronger complete tensor-analysis problems in Weinberg Chapter 4.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 2, parts (a)-(e), for the idealized spherical rotating planet and equatorial surface clock: calculate special-relativistic time dilation and its Earth value; Schwarzschild gravitational dilation and its Earth value; the lowest cross-correction in the full metric; the sea-level versus 2000 m mountain difference; and geosynchronous-satellite versus infinity and sea-level clock differences, retaining every supplied terrestrial constant and approximation order.
problems.short_topic: Earth, mountain, and satellite clock comparisons
problems.disposition_rationale: A rich Chapter 8 classic-tests parent that quantifies special-relativistic, gravitational, mixed, altitude, and orbital clock effects in a common model. All numerical data, trajectory definitions, and requested expansion orders are indispensable.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 3: in part (a) derive the near-Earth photon redshift from the equivalence principle through travel time, relative acceleration, and Doppler shift; in part (b) derive the same frequency ratio in general relativity and recover the Newtonian result.
problems.short_topic: Gravitational redshift from equivalence and metric methods
problems.disposition_rationale: The two independent derivations make a strong Chapter 3 parent and provide an internal physical check. The distance d, uniform-field approximation, boost step, and emitted/received-frequency comparison must remain together.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 4, parts (a)-(b), for a radial Schwarzschild geodesic with E=1 and rest at infinity: derive dt/dtau and dr/dtau; integrate r(tau); calculate infaller proper time between r=2R_* and the horizon r=R_*; and contrast this finite experience with the fixed-radius observer's Schwarzschild-time account.
problems.short_topic: Radial free fall through the Schwarzschild horizon
problems.disposition_rationale: A focused Chapter 8 parent contrasting proper and coordinate time at the horizon. The energy normalization, asymptotic initial condition, both radii, and interpretive comparison are essential.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 5 with its full equivalence-principle setup and Eqs. (1)-(8): part (a) reparameterizes an arbitrary null straight-line parameter into an affine one; part (b) transforms zero local-inertial acceleration into the global geodesic equation and provisional connection; part (c) derives metric-compatibility form from the local-inertial metric transformation; and part (d), using the printed permutation hint, obtains the Levi-Civita Christoffel formula.
problems.short_topic: Geodesic equation from the equivalence principle
problems.disposition_rationale: This unusually complete Chapter 3 derivation is explicitly modeled on Weinberg pp. 70-77 and treats null affine parameters without relying on path length. Every setup paragraph, intermediate equation, and hint is part of the logical chain.

documents.institution_or_author: Alan Guth, Massachusetts Institute of Technology

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 1: use the radial rest-at-infinity trajectory found in Problem Set 4 Problem 4 for an infaller passing a stationary observer one astronomical unit from a solar-mass black hole; decide whether finitely or infinitely many flashlight photons arrive before horizon crossing and whether they are red- or blueshifted; and, if finite, compute the external observer's total emission-time window.
problems.short_topic: Light signals sent to a Schwarzschild infaller
problems.disposition_rationale: A physically sharp Chapter 8 causal-redshift problem, but it has an explicit dependency on the radial trajectory from PS04 Problem 4. A selected version must insert that trajectory and its normalization rather than cite the earlier set.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 2: explicitly construct a single chart covering the infinite cylinder R times S^1, retaining the hint relating the noncontractible circular curve to the required chart image in R^2.
problems.short_topic: One-chart atlas for the infinite cylinder
problems.disposition_rationale: This is a pure point-set/topological chart construction with no tensor or gravitational development and no clear home in Weinberg Chapters 2-16. It remains inventoried as a complete source parent.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 3 with all definitions and transition data: part (a) proves the specified Mobius real-line bundle over S^1 has no nowhere-vanishing section; part (b) uses the fully printed four-chart torus atlas, ranges, identifications, and maps to construct a nowhere-zero tangent section; and part (c), with its northern/southern hint, gives a pictorial or verbal hairy-ball obstruction on S^2.
problems.short_topic: Nowhere-vanishing sections on Mobius, torus, and sphere bundles
problems.disposition_rationale: The parent is a substantial topology and vector-bundle exercise, but Weinberg's organization does not develop bundle topology or obstruction theory. Its lengthy transition functions and all three examples would have to be retained, making it unsuitable to force into Chapter 4.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 4, using the torus and fundamental domain defined in Problem 3(b): construct either a two-chart or three-chart atlas; for every chart give U_i, its image V_i, and the explicit coordinate map; and calculate one explicit overlap map between a chosen pair.
problems.short_topic: Two- or three-chart atlas for the torus
problems.disposition_rationale: This is another topology-specific atlas-construction parent outside Weinberg Chapters 2-16. It also explicitly depends on Problem 3(b)'s torus definition, so inventorying only its last-page requests would lose necessary source context.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 5, parts (a)-(c): derive the coordinate components of the commutator of vector fields and prove tensorial transformation despite partial derivatives; verify the two printed commuting fields and find coordinates in which they become coordinate-basis derivatives; and prove the Jacobi identity for three smooth vector fields.
problems.short_topic: Vector-field brackets, commuting frames, and Jacobi identity
problems.disposition_rationale: A coherent Chapter 4 parent linking the tensorial Lie bracket, integrability of a concrete commuting frame, and its algebraic Jacobi identity. All three stages and the explicit vector fields belong together.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 1 with Wald's functional definition of a tangent vector: part (a) proves constants are annihilated from linearity and Leibniz; part (b) uses the printed straight-line integral identity to construct H_mu(x), establish its value at p, and address smooth nonanalytic functions; and part (c) derives the coordinate differential-operator representation while justifying every step from the defining axioms.
problems.short_topic: Wald's derivation of tangent vectors as derivations
problems.disposition_rationale: A rigorous Chapter 4 parent proving equivalence between abstract derivations and coordinate tangent vectors. The integral construction, Taylor-series commentary, and explicit axiom checks are essential to avoid assuming the result.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 2 with the local-inertial coordinate conditions and metric transformation Eqs. (2.1)-(2.4): part (a) transforms the ordinary derivative of a contravariant vector and derives its connection term; part (b) identifies that term with the Levi-Civita symbols using metric derivatives; and part (c) repeats the derivation for a covector to obtain the opposite-sign connection term.
problems.short_topic: Covariant derivatives from locally inertial frames
problems.disposition_rationale: This complete Chapter 4 parent derives both vector and covector covariant derivatives directly from the equivalence-principle definition. All transformation formulas and both index types must be retained.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 3: for a two-sphere of radius A, part (a) calculates the metric, connection, Riemann tensor, Ricci tensor, and constant Ricci scalar; part (b) uses the Christoffel connection to find the direction change from counterclockwise parallel transport around any loop enclosing area A^2/10.
problems.short_topic: Curvature and finite holonomy of a two-sphere
problems.disposition_rationale: A strong Chapter 6 parent coupling a full curvature calculation to a geometric holonomy observable. The specified area and orientation in part (b) are necessary for the signed rotation result.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 4: for the printed upper-half-space metric a z^{-2}(dx^2+dy^2+dz^2), calculate the metric, connection, full Riemann tensor, Ricci tensor, and Ricci scalar.
problems.short_topic: Curvature of hyperbolic three-space
problems.disposition_rationale: This is a compact but complete constant-negative-curvature calculation for Chapter 6. Its full tensor hierarchy provides a useful contrast with the two-sphere parent rather than duplicating it.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 5: for the printed Schwarzschild metric and sphere element, use the complete supplied list of nonzero Christoffel symbols in part (a) to calculate every nonvanishing Riemann component, and in part (b) contract the result to show the Ricci tensor vanishes.
problems.short_topic: Riemann and Ricci tensors of Schwarzschild spacetime
problems.disposition_rationale: A direct Chapter 6 curvature audit of the Schwarzschild vacuum solution. The supplied connection list is a substantive hint that must remain with the full Riemann calculation and Ricci check.

documents.institution_or_author: Alan Guth, Massachusetts Institute of Technology

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 1: follow the supplied oriented infinitesimal parallelogram figure and parallel-transport definition to second order in epsilon, proving delta V^rho=-epsilon^2 R^rho_{ sigma mu nu} V^sigma A^mu B^nu from the printed commutator and coordinate formulas, including the source's correction of Carroll's sign.
problems.short_topic: Infinitesimal holonomy and the Riemann tensor
problems.disposition_rationale: A foundational Chapter 6 parent with an essential supplied loop diagram, traversal orientation, and sign warning. Any selected version must reproduce the figure or equivalent directed-edge data and preserve the source's curvature convention.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 2 for north-going great-circle geodesics on a sphere: part (a) obtains exact and small-angle separations and their acceleration; parts (b)-(c) evaluate both sides of the printed geodesic-deviation equation componentwise; and part (d) applies the supplied metric-distance second-derivative identity, proves its second term vanishes, and checks agreement with part (a).
problems.short_topic: Geodesic deviation on a two-sphere
problems.disposition_rationale: A detailed Chapter 6 parent that compares coordinate relative acceleration with invariant separation. It explicitly depends on the sphere curvature calculated in PS06 Problem 3, so those curvature results must be inserted or rederived; Eq. (2.4), absent from the cited textbook, is printed and must be retained.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 3 for the printed negative-curvature upper-half-space metric and specified geodesic family: parts (a)-(b) calculate both sides of geodesic deviation at (s,t)=(0,0), using the supplied local power-series hint; part (c) reparameterizes by arc length, shows the extra metric-distance term vanishes, and verifies the remaining separation equation.
problems.short_topic: Geodesic deviation in hyperbolic space
problems.disposition_rationale: This complements the sphere parent with a nontrivial negatively curved family and parameterization issue. It depends on curvature from PS06 Problem 4 and semicircular geodesics from PS02 Problem 4, which must be made explicit in any self-contained Chapter 6 adaptation.

documents.institution_or_author: Alan Guth, Massachusetts Institute of Technology

problems.parent_scope: Complete revised Problem 1, parts (a)-(l), with every printed definition, correction, and constraint: derive deviation transport and evolution of B_{mu nu}; derive vorticity propagation; construct timelike and null hypersurface-initialized irrotational congruences in parts (d)-(f); trace to the expansion equation; prove the symmetric tensor's orthogonality; minimize its square by Lagrange multipliers for timelike and null tangents; and reduce strong and null energy conditions to the stated perfect-fluid inequalities.
problems.short_topic: Raychaudhuri equation for timelike and null congruences
problems.disposition_rationale: A comprehensive Chapter 6 parent spanning the complete Raychaudhuri derivation, congruence construction, sharp dimension-dependent bounds, and energy conditions. The revised wording, explicit corrections to Carroll, Eqs. (1)-(31), and all parts (a)-(l) are essential; shortening it would destroy the source's logical structure.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 1, parts (a)-(e), with the Kruskal metric, implicit r relation, first-quadrant transformation, and both supplied figures: extend the Schwarzschild transformation consistently to quadrants II-IV; numerically invert and plot r/(2GM) versus T^2-R^2; calculate proper time along the stated white-hole-to-black-hole trajectory; determine the appearance and disappearance of the Einstein-Rosen bridge; and numerically plot its throat radius versus throat-clock proper time.
problems.short_topic: Global Kruskal extension and Einstein-Rosen bridge evolution
problems.disposition_rationale: A major Chapter 8 parent combining analytic extension, coordinate conventions, numerical inversion, proper time, and wormhole slicing. Figure 1 fixes quadrant labels and Figure 2 supplies the bridge-slice sequence; both figures or equivalent data and both requested calculated plots must be preserved.

documents.institution_or_author: Alan Guth, Massachusetts Institute of Technology

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 1, parts (a)-(c), for a zero-temperature noninteracting neutron Fermi gas: derive relativistic energy density and pressure including two spin states; introduce every printed dimensionless variable and use the supplied TOV and mass equations to derive dk-tilde/dr-tilde; then numerically integrate to the zero-Fermi-momentum surface for central-density ratios X=0.5,1,2,4 and report stellar masses and radii in solar masses and kilometers, retaining the event-location hint.
problems.short_topic: TOV neutron stars with a degenerate-neutron equation of state
problems.disposition_rationale: A complete Chapter 11 stellar-structure parent linking microphysical equation of state, nondimensionalization, and numerical TOV solutions. It requires elementary quantum-statistical background, but the task states the degeneracy and review dependency; selection must retain rather than suppress that prerequisite and the numerical stopping condition.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 2 for the printed Kruskal metric and implicit r(T,R): part (a) derives analytic partial derivatives of r; part (b) obtains the radial R geodesic equation and verifies the specified R-dot=0 reduction; and part (c) determines the acceleration direction for instantaneous rest and whether nonzero R-dot can reverse it.
problems.short_topic: Radial geodesic equations in Kruskal coordinates
problems.disposition_rationale: A self-contained Chapter 8 coordinate-dynamics parent distinct from the global PS09 exercise. The implicit differentiation formulas, proper-time convention, special-case check, and qualitative acceleration question all belong together.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 1 for the static rotationally and translationally symmetric cosmic-string metric: part (a) solves the reduced 2+1 vacuum equations; part (b) transforms and interprets the conical metric; part (c) relates a prescribed 2pi/N holonomy to integrated source curvature and writes the exterior metric; and part (d), using the cigar and Gauss-Bonnet hints, finds the far metric, maximum number of particles/strings, and total spatial curvature.
problems.short_topic: Cosmic-string conical geometry and integrated curvature
problems.disposition_rationale: A strong Chapter 13 symmetry-and-geometry parent that carries Einstein equations through holonomy and global topology. It suggests reviewing PS03's cone solution, but the printed ansatz and hints make the task recoverable; any adaptation must supply the conical facts actually used.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 2: prove both printed identities for an arbitrary Killing field, namely the second-covariant-derivative curvature relation and invariance of the Ricci scalar along the Killing flow.
problems.short_topic: Killing-vector curvature identities
problems.disposition_rationale: The two connected identities form a concise Chapter 13 parent linking local Killing equations to curvature invariance. Neither statement duplicates a complete earlier MIT parent.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 3: in part (a) find a complete independent set of Killing vector fields of four-dimensional Minkowski spacetime; in part (b) find all five Killing fields of the printed gravitational-wave metric with arbitrary a(u), b(u), retaining the hints that K^u=0 and the warning about index positions.
problems.short_topic: Killing fields of Minkowski and plane-wave spacetimes
problems.disposition_rationale: A useful Chapter 13 comparison between maximal flat symmetry and the restricted symmetry of a wave geometry. The full sets, unspecified profile functions, five-field hint, and index warning are necessary source constraints.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 4: integrate the spatial volume element of the printed closed FRW metric over both hemispheres, using the stated angular ranges and the radial coordinate that runs from pole to equator separately on each half, and give the total volume as a function of a(t).
problems.short_topic: Spatial volume of a closed FRW universe
problems.disposition_rationale: A compact Chapter 14 cosmography parent whose main subtlety is the double coverage implied by the radial coordinate. The two-hemisphere instruction and all coordinate ranges must be retained to avoid the common factor-of-two error.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 1, parts (a)-(e): prove that exterior differentiation of a p-form is unchanged by replacing partial with Levi-Civita covariant derivatives and that d^2=0; derive **F=-F for the printed curved-spacetime Hodge and Levi-Civita conventions without setting g=-1; and expand F=dA and d(*F)=*J into all four Minkowski Maxwell equations using the supplied E and B component conventions.
problems.short_topic: Differential-form formulation of Maxwell equations
problems.disposition_rationale: A complete Chapter 4 forms exercise combining connection cancellation, nilpotence, curved-space Hodge duality, and both pairs of Maxwell equations. Every determinant and orientation convention is essential when converting to the edition's Levi-Civita notation.

problems.short_topic: Corrected Kerr horizon-orbit argument
problems.disposition_rationale: A strong Chapter 8 advanced-black-hole parent whose pedagogical value lies in correcting an overclaimed textbook result. The original quotation, conserved quantities, corrected radius bound, and timelike causal proof must all be preserved.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 3 for the printed charged Kerr metric, Delta_q, rho^2, and electromagnetic potential: part (a) computes the outer-horizon area; part (b) finds the maximum negative-energy fragment ratio L^(2)/|E^(2)| in a perturbative Penrose process; and part (c) proves that the process cannot decrease horizon area, retaining the uncharged-Kerr textbook hint.
problems.short_topic: Kerr-Newman horizon area and the Penrose process
problems.disposition_rationale: A complete Chapter 8 black-hole-mechanics parent with all metric and gauge-potential data supplied. The small-projectile approximation, negative-energy condition, optimization, and final area inequality are one connected argument.

documents.institution_or_author: Alan Guth, Massachusetts Institute of Technology

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 1, parts (a)-(c), with the printed Weinberg surface-energy formula: transform Schwarzschild from polar to Cartesian-like coordinates and determine f(r); expand h_{mu nu} through order 1/r^2; and evaluate the energy inside radius r, obtaining M plus the stated order-1/r correction and interpreting the r-to-infinity limit as ADM energy.
problems.short_topic: Total and ADM energy of Schwarzschild spacetime
problems.disposition_rationale: This parent directly follows Weinberg Section 7.6 and is an excellent Chapter 7 energy exercise. The posted Weinberg excerpt is an external aid, but the operative surface formula, coordinate definitions, metric, and required asymptotic order are all printed.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 2 with the Robertson-Walker metric, perfect-fluid tensor, both Friedmann equations, and conservation equation: part (a) normalizes nonzero spatial curvature to k=+1 or -1; parts (b)-(d) solve flat, open, and closed vacuum-energy scale factors and compare their zeros/minimum; and part (e) embeds de Sitter as the printed hyperboloid in 4+1 Minkowski space and derives the closed slicing with Robertson-Walker time depending only on T.
problems.short_topic: Flat, open, closed, and embedded de Sitter space
problems.disposition_rationale: A strong Chapter 16 parent showing that three apparently different cosmologies are slicings of one maximally symmetric spacetime. All Friedmann data, symmetry commentary, and the embedding construction are connected and must remain together.

problems.parent_scope: Complete Problem 3 with the full quantum-statistical explanation of imaginary-time periodicity and the printed Schwarzschild/Kruskal and static-de-Sitter metrics: part (a)(i)-(v) analytically continues Schwarzschild through Kruskal variables, derives Euclidean periodicity and Hawking temperature, and restores k_B,c,hbar; part (b) repeats the result by near-horizon conical regularity; and part (c) applies the same method to the de Sitter horizon to derive the Gibbons-Hawking temperature.
problems.short_topic: Euclidean continuation and black-hole/de Sitter temperatures
problems.disposition_rationale: This is a complete modern extension to Chapter 8, with the de Sitter comparison linking to Chapter 16. Its quantum-statistical preamble, trace derivation, cross-reference to PS09, every metric, nested subpart (a)(i)-(v), and both conical-regularity arguments are necessary dependencies rather than optional exposition.
